items.content:
[Exclusive] Samsung Takes Early Lead in Nvidia’s ‘NVHBM’ Following HBM4

Samsung Electronics is poised to secure a key supplier position for Nvidia’s customized high-bandwidth memory (HBM), dubbed “NVHBM.” Nvidia is pursuing a new AI memory strategy for its next-generation computing systems that favors fewer stacked DRAM layers and higher speeds rather than continuing to increase stack height.

According to industry sources on August 28, Samsung Electronics is developing an 8-high HBM4E, or seventh-generation HBM, product tailored to Nvidia’s requirements. The new design has a lower stack height than the 12-high and 16-high products Samsung had originally been preparing.

Nvidia has also asked Samsung to target speeds of 17–18Gbps per pin, roughly 20% higher than the 14.4Gbps speed of Samsung’s initial HBM4E samples. The product is expected to be used for NVHBM optimized for Nvidia’s proprietary NVLink technology specification unveiled a day earlier.

The adoption of an 8-high configuration runs counter to the conventional direction of HBM development. HBM capacity has historically increased by moving from 4-high to 8-high and then to 12-high stacks. As the number of layers rises, however, DRAM dies must be thinned and stacked with greater precision, increasing back-end process complexity and creating additional yield challenges.

An 8-high design, by contrast, reduces manufacturing complexity and makes it easier to produce HBM in larger volumes. The move is therefore seen as part of Nvidia’s strategy to alleviate memory supply constraints.

Instead, Nvidia plans to push memory speeds significantly higher. NVHBM could be introduced as early as Rubin Ultra, Nvidia’s next-generation AI GPU scheduled for launch next year.

Rubin Ultra will expand the scale of GPU interconnects from the current 72 GPUs to as many as 576, an eightfold increase. Nvidia’s strategy appears to be to accept lower memory capacity per GPU by reducing HBM stack height, while connecting hundreds of GPUs equipped with faster HBM into a single system to boost aggregate compute performance.

Samsung is considered to have a competitive advantage over SK hynix and Micron in the emerging custom-HBM market. NVHBM requires not only DRAM capabilities but also the ability to design and manufacture logic-based base dies. Samsung possesses both memory and system-semiconductor capabilities, allowing it to provide an integrated solution.

“Samsung has already demonstrated industry-leading speeds with HBM4, so it should be able to capitalize on its strengths as competition shifts toward speed rather than increasingly higher stack counts,” an industry source said.

items.content:
Korean media reported that SK hynix’s NAND flash business continues to struggle to narrow the productivity gap with Samsung Electronics and other competitors, as it lags in transitioning older production lines to newer process generations.

As of the second quarter of this year, older-generation processes such as 176-layer NAND still accounted for more than half of SK hynix’s production, while Samsung Electronics had already completed the transition of its main production generation to 236-layer NAND.

The 176-layer generation currently accounts for around 50% of SK hynix’s NAND production in the second quarter. This high dependence on 176-layer NAND puts the company at a cost disadvantage because it produces relatively fewer bits per wafer.

Some analysts also say that although SK hynix has emphasized progress on its technology roadmap, including expanding the share of 300-layer-class NAND, this has yet to translate clearly into revenue performance.

NAND flash improves both capacity and cost efficiency by vertically stacking memory cells that store data. The greater the number of layers, the more data can be stored on a wafer of the same area, improving both output per wafer and cost competitiveness. Companies that fail to migrate to next-generation processes must therefore use more wafers and devote more production-line operating time to produce the same volume, inevitably placing them at a disadvantage in terms of profitability.

As of the end of the second quarter, 236-layer NAND accounted for more than 60% of Samsung Electronics’ production, establishing it as the company’s main production generation. Although both SK hynix and Samsung Electronics have NAND generations in the low-to-mid-200-layer range, there is a clear gap in the speed at which they have transitioned to mass production.

“Samsung Electronics is pursuing a strategy of concentrating production volumes in a specific generation to improve both yields and costs, whereas SK hynix operates multiple generations simultaneously, which inevitably reduces the relative efficiency of its production-line operations,” an industry official said.

SK hynix’s current NAND production structure also trails those of Micron and China’s YMTC, in addition to Samsung Electronics. According to market research firm Omdia, as of the end of the second quarter, 232-layer NAND accounted for 53% of Micron’s production, while the next-generation 276-layer product had expanded to 33%. At YMTC, 232-layer NAND represented 68% of production, indicating that the company had already established a production system centered on advanced processes.

At Kioxia and Sandisk, 162-layer BiCS6 accounted for 37% of production and 112-layer BiCS5 for 34% as of the second quarter, meaning older-generation processes still made up roughly 70% of total production. While their generation mix may appear similar to that of SK hynix, the share of their latest-generation BiCS8, a 218-layer product, nearly tripled in just two quarters, rising from 9% in the fourth quarter of last year to 24% in the second quarter of this year. Their transition pace is therefore considered relatively fast.

This trend is also evident in revenue market share.

According to industry sources, SK hynix’s NAND revenue share, including Solidigm, rose to 21.4% in the fourth quarter of last year before plunging by nearly 5 percentage points to 16.4% in the first quarter of this year. Over the same period, China’s YMTC increased its share from 11.5% to 16.2%, nearly catching up with SK hynix. Some interpret this as evidence that SK hynix may have had relatively limited capacity to respond with additional volumes during a period of rising NAND prices.

“When prices are rising, a higher share of newer-generation products allows increases in selling prices to combine with cost improvements, producing a greater uplift in profit margins,” an industry official said. “SK hynix’s market-share decline should be viewed not simply as a volume issue, but as the result of delays in its process-generation transition.”

The official added, however, that “given the recent continued rise in NAND prices, the impact on the company’s overall earnings is limited.”

items.content:
From Marvell’s conference call:

Q: What progress are you seeing in CXL and scale-up optics?
A: CXL began as a server-centric memory architecture but has ultimately proven to be ideally suited for memory expansion and inference. It is now being deployed at scale by multiple hyperscalers. Amid growing inference demand and memory scarcity, customers are revising their plans to expand their use of the technology. Marvell also secured additional design wins in the latest quarter. Scale-up optics has accelerated further from the roughly $300 million FY28 outlook provided last quarter, including $150 million from Celestial AI CPO. CPO and NPO are not an either-or choice; both will coexist.

Q: How are constraints such as surging memory prices affecting design wins?
A: As supply, power, and architectural constraints converge, the need for fungibility across compute, networking, and memory is increasing. The ability to execute rapidly on custom and semi-custom solutions—and modify products to adapt to evolving architectures—is a critical asset. CXL memory expansion and AI inference accelerators are representative examples. Activity is increasing significantly as the market rapidly shifts from training to inference and then to monetization.
